text: [{"id":2,"latex":"Individual Subjectivism: $x$ is right = I (the speaker) approve of $x$."},{"id":3,"latex":"Cultural Relativism: $x$ is right = Society approves of $x$."},{"id":4,"latex":"Divine Command Theory: $x$ is right = God approves of $x$."},{"id":5,"latex":"Third, these theories make moral disagreement difficult to understand. On the individual subjectivist view, $A$ could disagree with $B$'s statement, '$x$ is wrong', only if $A$ doubted that $B$ was truthfully reporting $B$'s attitudes. On the cultural relativist view, the disagreement could only occur if the parties disagreed about what the attitudes of most of society were, and it would be impossible for anyone to criticize the prevailing social norms. On the divine command theory, moral disagreements would have to be disagreements about God's commands, and atheists and agnostics thus could not have moral views.$^1$"},{"id":6,"latex":"Fourth, these theories all imply that a merely arbitrary attitude or decision can render an action obligatory. All of them imply that there are no evaluative facts independent of the attitudes of the specified individual or group. Therefore, the specified individual or group can not approve of the things they approve of because they are right, good, or have any other positive characteristic. Thus, these attitudes of approval would have to be arbitrary. But how would someone's arbitrarily approving of $x$ make it right to do $x$?"}]
